title: Australia has a new AI model that could give Anthropic a challenge
full_text:
As Anthropic tries to convince Australian investors that its booming artificial intelligence platforms make it a $2 trillion company, a Canberra-based AI company backed by less than $10 million in external funding has developed a new model it says can win business off the US giants.
Trellis Data will unveil its new Agentaus 1 model on Thursday, which at about 220 billion parameters is 50 per cent bigger than its previous model, and the company claims it performs well on most tasks professionals use AI for.
In AI models, a parameter is a unit that marks reasoning capability, and Agentaus 1 has significantly fewer than the latest frontier models from Anthropic. But Trellis founder Michael Gately said its models were less than a year behind Anthropic's in terms of capability, and could provide cheaper, locally based artificial intelligence that is good enough.
"On benchmarking we are sitting at 43rd in the world, which may not seem super high, but we are lagging the frontier models by four to six months, and customers are getting just as good results with us for what they need to do," said Gately.
"Most of us aren't trying to do breakthrough scientific research or travel to Mars, and for those that just want to run their business, Agentaus provides a cheaper and safer alternative in terms of data privacy than the alternatives," he said.
Trellis has been in the tech scene since 2016, and has previously specialised in applying AI technology to high-security environments across government, intelligence, defence and law enforcement. The company's models are now targeting general users as well.
It was backed by CSIRO's venture capital fund, Main Sequence, in a $3 million funding round in 2020. And Gately said it was planning to raise more capital to keep its model's progress going, but that it needed nowhere near as much as its rivals in the United States.
"We have been building our models for 10 years, but now there are methods to accelerate, and the ability to build models at a cheaper price is definitely a reason for us to be able to achieve our goals," he said.
"But we do need substantial additional investment, and we're imminently going to market for that.
"It's going to be in the eight-figure range, and we already have a number of investors interested, so whether it's this side of Christmas or in the New Year, it will be relatively quick," said Gately.
The subject of whether Australia needs to have sovereign AI capability in the form of native models has been contentious in the local industry. Some in the industry have said it is pointless for firms to try and compete with the multibillion-dollar investment efforts of the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI. However, incidents such as the US government blocking international access to the latest Anthropic models due to its cybersecurity capabilities this year have led to industry calls for Australian-based alternatives.
"I definitely believe we need Australian foundational models trained on Australian intellectual property. What happened in the Strait of Hormuz with the supply of oil to Australia could happen to us with data," said Ben Thompson, the co-founder of Australian human resources technology unicorn Employment Hero.
"The Anthropic block outside of the US was a really important moment that we should all be looking at and thinking about how exposed we are as a country if we are dependent on offshore models for all of the work we're going to be doing in the future," he said.
Other companies attempting to build local AI models include Sovereign Australia AI, which is developing a model called Ginan, and Maincode, which has a model called Matilda.
Will Liang, founder of advisory firm Amplify AI, has not had the chance to test Agentaus 1 yet, but said he believed it would be very difficult for Trellis to make significant commercial inroads given the global competition.
Liang said the argument for data sovereignty was becoming less compelling as a differentiator as Amazon Web Services, Google and Microsoft already supported Australian-based AI services for selected international models, and organisations could deploy international open-weight models, including Chinese models, on Australian-controlled infrastructure. "This means Australian businesses don't necessarily need an Australian-developed foundation model to keep sensitive data and AI processing within Australia," he said.
"There are exceptions where I can see a genuine market, like defence, intelligence and certain highly sensitive government applications, which may place a premium on independent control over the underlying technology, including the ability to operate without relying on foreign providers," said Liang.
As it stands, Agentaus is a proprietary model, but Gately said an open-weights version was being considered by the company.
He said its new ranking to be published on AI industry benchmarking platform MMLU-Pro made Agentaus 1 Australia's best-performing general AI model.
Gately said he was prepared for naysayers to take potshots at attempts to create globally significant AI models in Australia, but said the country needed local options to thrive.
"Australia needs to be able to stand on its own two feet ... The global economy is not as global as it once was and we are seeing fragmentation from Europe, Canada, India, and other places as well, where they are wanting to have their own AI models," he said.
"Australia needs something in its backyard that it can depend on," said Gately. "Also in the US, there are start-ups getting funded to build AI models every month, and nobody is telling them they shouldn't bother because of the bigger rivals," he said.
Nine Entertainment Co.
